The Renaissance in Lyon concerns the history of the city of Lyon during the Renaissance.

It began in the middle of the 15th century with the establishment of the Fairs of Lyon by the French king Charles VII. This event placed the city at the center of major European commerce and revitalized the former episcopal city.

Numerous foreigners, especially Italians, soon settled in the city, which became an important center of Renaissance culture, with significant banking and publishing activities. This era also saw the introduction and early development of the silk industry.

During the Wars of Religion, the city experienced a brief Protestant occupation, followed by the Lyonnais vespers, a massacre of Protestants in the wake of the St. Initially aligned with the Catholic League, Lyon submitted to King Henry IV after his conversion to Catholicism, the king subsequently reformed the consulate to secure the city's loyalty.
The city and its inhabitants

The city along the Rhône experienced significant demographic and urban expansion during the Renaissance. While its boundaries did not expand substantially, it densified through the raising of buildings and the subdivision of undeveloped areas. Supported by increasing prosperity, numerous stone structures were erected, though no large prestigious public buildings appeared.

The most prominent Lyonnais institution was the consulate, which connected with the populace primarily through the pennons for policing duties and the General Alms for welfare. The political landscape was rounded out by the governor and the foreign nations.
Topography and architecture

Driven by sustained prosperity, the city continually developed and rebuilt itself. Its overall layout remained largely unchanged, rather than sprawling outward, it densified inward. Gardens gradually shrank, and houses were rebuilt on-site with additional stories. However, the southern part of the Peninsula and the hill slopes remained unurbanized.

Faced with the evolving functions and socio-economic significance of their city, the consulate sought to adapt a still typically medieval urbanism (narrow streets, few public squares, homogeneous neighborhoods) to new demands.

Over the 150 years of the Lyonnais Renaissance, the city's elites successfully transformed it: neighborhoods became distinct and specialized, public squares emerged, and key thoroughfares were improved. Nevertheless, they failed to achieve their ambition of glorifying the city with monumental works, as was seen in other major European cities of the era.
Morphology of civil buildings

The rise in inhabitants per household coincided with the economic surge beginning around 1460. The right bank of the Saône, in particular, underwent a wave of demolitions to make way for taller, more opulent structures. Cultivated spaces vanished during this period, and throughout the 16th century, any building capable of being heightened was raised.

Until the 1500s, architectural styles drew from Gothic influences, later evolving into an eclectic blend of various elements. The city's wealth enabled a renewal of Gothic building art, though the Renaissance style did not become predominant.

This intense densification gave rise to traboules, private passages that, by necessity, became semi-public thoroughfares of ambiguous status, used by pedestrians navigating the narrow, congested streets.

Obtaining a comprehensive view of house morphologies from this era is (still) challenging, as even the extensive Old Lyon district features many partially rebuilt structures from later centuries. Generally, buildings were narrow (five to six meters wide) and deep (up to twenty meters), typically with two stories.
Many connected to a rear building, sometimes up to four in total (as in the "Grande Traboule"), linked by galleries at each level, accessible via spiral staircases.

Alongside these ordinary residences, numerous luxurious homes emerged from the 15th century onward, such as the Maison de la Rose on Rue Mercière, owned by the councilor Ennemond de Syvrieu and later by Jacques Cœur. The grandest residences incorporating Renaissance elements, however, dated to the 16th century.
These elite homes illustrated the gradual fusion of medieval Gothic with ancient motifs drawn from Italian Renaissance architecture.
General evolutions
Despite resistance and the consulate's lack of consistent resources, numerous changes in the urban fabric were evident across four successive phases.

From the mid-15th century to 1500, the city densified without significant new builds, primarily by elevating existing structures. Prosperity returned in the 1460s, but recovery from the Hundred Years' War took time.

In 1468, 1470, the consulate authorized some constructions on Rue Mercière or at the Saulnerie, concurrently, it contemplated demolishing the Saint-Vincent borough to bolster northern defenses or permitted the demolition of an alley to expand the Grandes Carmes cloister.
Visible signs of urban evolution included the opening of two Saône ports: Saint-Éloi (1482, 1483) and Saint-Paul (1485, 1490).

From 1500 to 1540, new builds occupied wastelands and gardens. The city densification eliminated open spaces, resuming the horizontal expansion that had been interrupted since the mid-13th century. Only between 1540 and 1560 did systematic road rationalization begin, accompanied by the creation of new public squares.

Finally, from 1560 to 1600, despite some alterations by the Protestant authorities for military circulation on major routes, urban development stabilized amid political and economic crises that limited resources.

Lyon lacked a political force strong enough to mobilize capital, champion large projects, and overcome opposition, as was the case in Paris or major Italian cities, explaining the absence of monumental civic buildings.
Several mid-16th-century proposals made at the peak of prosperity, such as rebuilding Place du Change (the center of Lyonnais business) or erecting a civic palace, were not carried out.
= Urban transformations =

Lyon had to accommodate a larger, wealthier population and a massive influx of people and goods four times yearly during the fairs. This adaptation involved conflicts and resistance, with key changes enforced by the Protestant consulate, implementing long-debated measures.

At Fourvière's base, the canons' cloister at Saint-Jean Cathedral was forcibly opened by Baron des Adrets, who razed its walls in 1562. On the Peninsula, convent and church cemeteries became squares: Jacobins (1562), Cordeliers (1567), and Saint-Nizier (1593). The present-day Place Bellecour area served as military ground, redeveloped multiple times.

At Croix-Rousse's foot, the ancient Terreaux ditch was filled to enable urban extension downhill. Similarly, the fortified Saint-Just cloister was dismantled from May to September, though it had been planned since 1525. These efforts, eliminating wall vulnerabilities and creating drill squares, prepared for anticipated conflict.

The traditional traversal axis, Rhône bridge, rues Bourgchanin, Confort, Mercière, and Saône bridge, was duplicated by one via Rhône bridge, Rue de la Barre, Place Bellecour, Port du Roi, Saône ferries, Port des Estres, rues Bombarde and Chemin-Neuf. Other streets were also developed.

From the late 14th century, the consulate pursued a public water policy, securing concessions for religious-controlled sources to augment its own. The oldest public sources, Choulans, Saint-Épipoy, and la Chana, were supplemented in 1396 by fountains at Saint-Marcel, Sainte-Catherine, and des Gardes.

In 1504, 1506, Choulans sources were partially diverted to supply Saint-Laurent-des-Vignes hospital and three new fountains at la Blancherie, Maison Athanase, and Jardin des Fleur de Lys. By 1530, the city had about fifteen public fountains: twelve on the Saône's right bank and three on the left.
= Socio-economic evolutions =

Urban activity locations also shifted. The main cattle market, sited on Rue Juiverie until 1490 amid an expanding business district, relocated to Place de la Croix de Colle. Similarly, the pig market moved from the center in 1513 to the Lanterne ditches.

Slaughterhouses likewise shifted early in the 16th century from Saint-Paul and Saint-Nizier to Place de Bourg Neuf and the filled Lanterne ditches. These changes reflected municipal efforts to move polluting activities to the periphery, allowing the center to concentrate on residential use and reducing sources and spread of disease.
The city's neighborhoods

By the late 15th century, the densest areas were the Saône's right bank and, on the Peninsula, a bourgeois urban core along the era's Rue Mercière (via mercatoria), spanning from Saône to Rhône bridge. Corporations, trades, and foreign nations clustered tightly in neighborhoods or streets, reflecting Lyon's strong social organization.
= Saint-Georges, Saint-Jean, and the Roanne palace neighborhood =

Fourvière's lower slopes were narrow, topography-constrained. Main streets ran parallel to the river, with limited cross-ways. Upper slopes were nearly uninhabited, covered in woods, gardens, and vines.
